questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

content.content: --- title: "Naming: Versions in Filenames" dc:title: "Naming: Versions in Filenames" dc:creator: "Christopher Steel" dc:contributor: "Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), AI assistance" dc:subject: "naming, versions, filenames, D1" dc:description: "Before 1.0.0 a versioned document's filename ends in -vX.Y.Z with dots, matching its sat:version; from 1.0.0 the filename carries no version; the hyphenated form -vX-Y-Z is never used." dc:date: "2026-10-09" dc:type: "Text" dc:format: "text/markdown" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:da71b33c-cd19-4a36-bdcb-cba940739632" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" sat:version: "0.1.0" sat:status: "In force" sat:directive: "naming/versions-in-filenames" sat:enforced_by: - "conformance.naming.versions_in_filenames" --- # Naming: Versions in Filenames Version: 0.1.0 Status: In force ## Rule A versioned document is one under a language's `docs/` whose front matter carries `sat:version`. Templates, schemas, configuration, licence texts and code are versioned by the repository's release and carry no version in their names. - Below 1.0.0, its filename ends in `-v` and its version with dots, before the extension, and that version equals `sat:version`: `directory-guide-v0.2.0.md` holds `sat:version: "0.2.0"`. - From 1.0.0, its filename carries no version: `directory-guide.md`. The version lives in front matter, the Changelog table and git tags. - No filename anywhere uses the hyphenated form, such as `-v0-2-0`. A version bump renames the file with `git mv` and updates links to it in the same commit. Tools find the version with the pattern `-v(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)` immediately before the extension, never by splitting the name on dots. ## Rationale This is decision D1, recorded as uc-automa 0002. The hyphenated form came from an earlier assumption and has had to be corrected several times; the check makes the correction permanent. ## Examples | Filename | Front matter | Verdict | | --- | --- | --- | | `0001--licensing-v0.1.0.md` | `sat:version: "0.1.0"` | Conforms | | `0001--licensing.md` | `sat:version: "0.1.0"` | Missing suffix below 1.0.0 | | `0001--licensing-v0.1.0.md` | `sat:version: "0.2.0"` | Suffix does not match | | `guide-v1.0.0.md` | `sat:version: "1.0.0"` | Version in the filename from 1.0.0 | | `guide-v0-1-0.md` | any | Hyphenated version | ## Check `conformance.naming.versions_in_filenames` reports any hyphenated version in any name, and compares every Markdown document's filename with its `sat:version`. The layout check accepts a decision record without a suffix, because `{version}` is optional in the layout to allow for 1.0.0 and later; this check catches the record that is still below 1.0.0. Its fixtures are under `tests/fixtures/conformance/naming/versions-in-filenames/`, including that exact case. ## Changelog | Version | Date | Status | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0.1.0 | 2026-10-09 | In force | Initial version | ## License This document, *Naming: Versions in Filenames*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). ====== Version: 0.1.0 Status: Accepted ## Context Versioned documents across Vishpala's repositories carried their version in the filename in a hyphenated form, such as -v0-1-0, which came from an earlier AI assumption, not from the spec, and had to be corrected several times. #!/usr/bin/env python3
# check-conformance.py
"""
check-conformance.py, report mechanically-detectable conformance issues.

Scans versioned markdown documents under en/docs and reports the findings
that a machine can detect without judgement, the class of issue collected
in ROADMAP.md: dotted filename version separators, missing required
frontmatter fields, a dc:identifier that does not match the filename
slug, em dashes in prose, asterisk bullets, and numbered headings.

This is a linter, not an autofixer. It changes nothing. It exits non-zero
if any issue is found, so it can gate a commit or run in CI.

Usage:
    check-conformance.py            check en/docs under this script's directory
    check-conformance.py PATH ...   check the given files or directories
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
DOCS = ROOT / "en" / "docs"

REQUIRED_FIELDS = [
    "dc:title",
    "dcterms:version",
    "dc:creator",
    "dc:identifier",
    "dcterms:created",
    "dcterms:modified",
    "sat:uuid",
]

DOTTED_VERSION = re.compile(r"-v\d+\.\d+\.\d+")
HYPHEN_VERSION_SUFFIX = re.compile(r"-v\d+-\d+-\d+$")
NUMBERED_HEADING = re.compile(r"^#{1,6}\s+\d+([.)]|\s)")
ASTERISK_BULLET = re.compile(r"^\s*\*\s+\S")
IDENTIFIER_LINE = re.compile(r'^dc:identifier:\s*"?([^"\n]+)"?\s*$')


def split_frontmatter(text: str):
    """Return (frontmatter_lines, body_lines). Frontmatter is empty if absent."""
    lines = text.splitlines()
    if not lines or lines[0].strip() != "---":
        return [], lines
    for i in range(1, len(lines)):
        if lines[i].strip() == "---":
            return lines[1:i], lines[i + 1:]
    return [], lines


def body_without_code(body_lines):
    """Yield (line_number, line) for body lines outside fenced code blocks."""
    in_fence = False
    for offset, line in enumerate(body_lines):
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith("```") or stripped.startswith("~~~"):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            continue
        if not in_fence:
            yield offset, line


def slug_from_filename(name: str) -> str:
    stem = name[:-3] if name.endswith(".md") else name
    return re.sub(r"-v\d+[-.]\d+[-.]\d+$", "", stem)


def check_file(path: Path):
    issues = []
    name = path.name
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    fm_lines, body_lines = split_frontmatter(text)
    has_fm = bool(fm_lines)

    if DOTTED_VERSION.search(name):
        issues.append("filename uses dotted version separator; use hyphens (v0-1-0)")

    if has_fm:
        joined_fm = "\n".join(fm_lines)
        for field in REQUIRED_FIELDS:
            if not re.search(rf"^{re.escape(field)}:", joined_fm, re.MULTILINE):
                issues.append(f"missing required frontmatter field: {field}")

        identifier = None
        for line in fm_lines:
            m = IDENTIFIER_LINE.match(line)
            if m:
                identifier = m.group(1).strip()
                break
        if identifier is not None:
            expected = slug_from_filename(name)
            if identifier != expected:
                issues.append(
                    f"dc:identifier {identifier!r} does not match filename slug {expected!r}"
                )

    # Body checks, skipping fenced code blocks.
    for offset, line in body_without_code(body_lines):
        lineno = offset + len(fm_lines) + (2 if has_fm else 0) + 1
        if "—" in line:
            issues.append(f"line {lineno}: em dash in prose (use commas)")
        if ASTERISK_BULLET.match(line):
            issues.append(f"line {lineno}: asterisk bullet (use '-')")
        if NUMBERED_HEADING.match(line):
            issues.append(f"line {lineno}: numbered heading (see Markdown: No Heading Numbers)")

    return issues


def iter_markdown(targets):
    for target in targets:
        if target.is_dir():
            yield from sorted(target.rglob("*.md"))
        elif target.suffix == ".md":
            yield target

    args = sys.argv[1:]
    targets = [Path(a) for a in args] if args else [DOCS]
    files = list(iter_markdown(targets))
    if not files:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# check-conformance.py
"""
check-conformance.py, report mechanically-detectable conformance issues.

Scans versioned markdown documents under en/docs and reports the findings
that a machine can detect without judgement, the class of issue collected
in ROADMAP.md: dotted filename version separators, missing required
frontmatter fields, a dc:identifier that does not match the filename
slug, em dashes in prose, asterisk bullets, and numbered headings.

This is a linter, not an autofixer. It changes nothing. It exits non-zero
if any issue is found, so it can gate a commit or run in CI.

Usage:
    check-conformance.py            check en/docs under this script's directory
    check-conformance.py PATH ...   check the given files or directories
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
DOCS = ROOT / "en" / "docs"

REQUIRED_FIELDS = [
    "dc:title",
    "dcterms:version",
    "dc:creator",
    "dc:identifier",
    "dcterms:created",
    "dcterms:modified",
    "sat:uuid",
]

DOTTED_VERSION = re.compile(r"-v\d+\.\d+\.\d+")
HYPHEN_VERSION_SUFFIX = re.compile(r"-v\d+-\d+-\d+$")
NUMBERED_HEADING = re.compile(r"^#{1,6}\s+\d+([.)]|\s)")
ASTERISK_BULLET = re.compile(r"^\s*\*\s+\S")
IDENTIFIER_LINE = re.compile(r'^dc:identifier:\s*"?([^"\n]+)"?\s*$')


def split_frontmatter(text: str):
    """Return (frontmatter_lines, body_lines). Frontmatter is empty if absent."""
    lines = text.splitlines()
    if not lines or lines[0].strip() != "---":
        return [], lines
    for i in range(1, len(lines)):
        if lines[i].strip() == "---":
            return lines[1:i], lines[i + 1:]
    return [], lines


def body_without_code(body_lines):
    """Yield (line_number, line) for body lines outside fenced code blocks."""
    in_fence = False
    for offset, line in enumerate(body_lines):
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith("```") or stripped.startswith("~~~"):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            continue
        if not in_fence:
            yield offset, line


def slug_from_filename(name: str) -> str:
    stem = name[:-3] if name.endswith(".md") else name
    return re.sub(r"-v\d+[-.]\d+[-.]\d+$", "", stem)


def check_file(path: Path):
    issues = []
    name = path.name
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    fm_lines, body_lines = split_frontmatter(text)
    has_fm = bool(fm_lines)

    if DOTTED_VERSION.search(name):
        issues.append("filename uses dotted version separator; use hyphens (v0-1-0)")

    if has_fm:
        joined_fm = "\n".join(fm_lines)
        for field in REQUIRED_FIELDS:
            if not re.search(rf"^{re.escape(field)}:", joined_fm, re.MULTILINE):
                issues.append(f"missing required frontmatter field: {field}")

        identifier = None
        for line in fm_lines:
            m = IDENTIFIER_LINE.match(line)
            if m:
                identifier = m.group(1).strip()
                break
        if identifier is not None:
            expected = slug_from_filename(name)
            if identifier != expected:
                issues.append(
                    f"dc:identifier {identifier!r} does not match filename slug {expected!r}"
                )

    # Body checks, skipping fenced code blocks.
    for offset, line in body_without_code(body_lines):
        lineno = offset + len(fm_lines) + (2 if has_fm else 0) + 1
        if "—" in line:
            issues.append(f"line {lineno}: em dash in prose (use commas)")
        if ASTERISK_BULLET.match(line):
            issues.append(f"line {lineno}: asterisk bullet (use '-')")
        if NUMBERED_HEADING.match(line):
            issues.append(f"line {lineno}: numbered heading (see Markdown: No Heading Numbers)")

    return issues


def iter_markdown(targets):
    for target in targets:
        if target.is_dir():
            yield from sorted(target.rglob("*.md"))
        elif target.suffix == ".md":
            yield target

sat:changelog:
  - version: "0.1.0"
    date: "2026-08-12"
    author: "Christopher Steel"
    notes: >
      Initial draft. Written after a repository audit found two competing
      version postfix forms split by location, dotted inside radar/ and
      hyphenated everywhere else, with no directive stating which was
      correct. The hyphenated form was already implied by the file naming
      section of the web-ready APA 7 style guide but was stated only as an
      example, so it did not survive contact with a directory that had
      drifted. This directive states the rule directly and adds the
      drop-at-1.0.0 half, which was not previously recorded anywhere.
### Version suffixes

Version suffixes follow `automa/versioning/defaults/versioning-postfix-rules-v0-1-0.md`. A document below 1.0.0 carries its version as a hyphenated postfix, `<title-slug>-v0-1-0.md`. At 1.0.0 the postfix is dropped and the filename becomes stable.

An earlier version of this roadmap recorded that documents inside `radar/` used a dotted form, `-v0.1.0`. That was an accurate description of the directory at the time but not a rule, and the repository has since been normalized to the hyphenated form throughout.

Only the radar evaluation in this directory currently carries a version suffix. The phase documents carry none. Adding suffixes to them is deferred until they leave Draft status, because renaming now would break the cross-references recorded in this roadmap.

## Version Control Integration
## File naming

Radar entries diverge from the SAT file-naming convention. An entry filename is its slug joined to a short tagline by a double hyphen, with no version suffix:

```text
dual-mode-language-authority--standard-aware-not-standard-dependent.md
```
*Style Guide: Versioned Documents in Unrendered Markdown* is authoritative for document structure, filename patterns, frontmatter schema, and closing sections across the repository. The register-and-audience guides (*Technical Documentation for Technologists*, *Plain Language for General Audiences*, *Web-Ready Unrendered Markdown Using APA 7*, and *Navigation and Accessibility*) govern voice, register, audience, citation practice, and heading semantics, and defer to the versioned-documents guide

The alternative considered was a flat set of peers with no designated authority, which is the state that produced the contradictions this roadmap catalogues. It was rejected because overlapping rules with no tie-breaker cannot be resolved except by rewriting one guide to match another arbitrarily. A named authority makes every later reconciliation a deference rather than a negotiation.

### D2: Filename version separator

Hyphens, always: `v0-1-0`, never `v0.1.0`. The alternative, the plain-language guide's rationale that dots keep the version machine-detectable, was answered rather than overruled silently: a hyphenated suffix is equally machine-detectable with a fixed pattern (`-v\d+-\d+-\d+`), and the double-hyphen semantic separator already gives the repository a consistent hyphen grammar. Dotted versions in filenames are now caught by the conformance checker.

### D3: Numbered body sections

# Markdown: Versioned Document Filenames

Version: 0.2.0
Status: Draft
Style Guide: style-guide--versioned-documents-in-unrendered-markdown

## Abstract

This directive states how a versioned markdown document is named on disk while its version is below 1.0.0, including documents published in more than one variant, such as two layouts of the same source. It exists so that an AI collaborator names files correctly by default, at generation time, rather than inferring a pattern from whatever filenames happen to be in front of it.

## The rule

Before version 1.0.0, a versioned document's filename is its identifier, followed by a version separator, followed by its version written with a lowercase `v` and dots, followed by `.md`.

The version separator is a single hyphen, unless the identifier ends with a variant segment, in which case it is a double hyphen:

```text
<slug>-v<major>.<minor>.<patch>.md
<slug>--<variant>--v<major>.<minor>.<patch>.md
```

## Segments and separators

A double hyphen (`--`) separates the major segments of a name. A single hyphen joins the words within a segment. Two kinds of double-hyphen segment exist, and only one of them affects the version separator.

A category prefix comes first and states what kind of document this is, such as `markdown--`, `style-guide--`, or a source-document code such as `dge-60-vf--`. A category prefix does not change the version separator: `markdown--no-heading-numbers` is versioned as `markdown--no-heading-numbers-v0.4.1.md`.

A variant segment comes last and distinguishes one form of a document from another form of the same document, such as `--original-layout` and `--balise-layout`. When the identifier ends with a variant segment, the version separator is a double hyphen, so the version reads as a segment of its own: `...--balise-layout--v0.1.0.md`.

## Where each part comes from

The identifier is the document's `dc:identifier`, which never carries a version but does carry any variant segment. The version is the document's `dcterms:version`, prefixed with `v`. The two must agree: a document whose frontmatter says `dc:identifier: "example--balise-layout"` and `dcterms:version: "0.1.0"` is saved as `example--balise-layout--v0.1.0.md`.

Variants of the same document point at each other with `dc:relation`, naming the other variant's identifier.

When the version changes, the filename changes with it. Updating `dcterms:version` without renaming the file, or renaming the file without updating `dcterms:version`, leaves the document inconsistent. The same applies to adding, removing, or renaming a variant segment, which changes `dc:identifier` as well.

## Examples

Correct:

```text
markdown--no-heading-numbers-v0.4.1.md
style-guide--markdown-mermaid-navigation-flowcharts-and-linked-sections-v0.1.5.md
markdown--versioned-document-filenames-v0.2.0.md
dge-60-vf--scrutateur-et-secretaire-du-bureau-de-vote--original-layout--v0.2.1.md
dge-60-vf--scrutateur-et-secretaire-du-bureau-de-vote--balise-layout--v0.1.0.md
```

Incorrect:

| Filename | Problem |
| --- | --- |
| `markdown--no-heading-numbers-v0_4_1.md` | Underscores instead of dots |
| `markdown--no-heading-numbers-v0-4-1.md` | Hyphens instead of dots |
| `markdown--no-heading-numbers-0.4.1.md` | Missing the `v` |
| `markdown--no-heading-numbers_v0.4.1.md` | Underscore instead of a hyphen before the version |
| `markdown--no-heading-numbers--v0.4.1.md` | Double hyphen before the version without a variant segment; a category prefix does not count |
| `example--balise-layout-v0.1.0.md` | Single hyphen before the version after a variant segment |
| `markdown--no-heading-numbers.md` | Missing the version suffix before 1.0.0 |

Copies of documents whose filenames show underscored or hyphenated versions are not evidence of the convention. Name new and revised files by this rule, not by the pattern of nearby files.

## Scope

This directive covers versions below 1.0.0 only. The filename convention at 1.0.0 and later is not defined here.

## License

This document, *Markdown: Versioned Document Filenames*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 or later](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.html).

| Version | Status | Notes |
|---------|--------|-------|
| 0.2.0 | Draft | Added trailing variant segments, which take a double-hyphen version separator; distinguished them from leading category prefixes, which do not; variant segments belong in `dc:identifier`, and variants point at each other with `dc:relation` |
| 0.1.0 | Draft | Initial draft; states the pre-1.0.0 filename convention `<slug>-v0.1.0.md` after an underscored suffix was inferred from uploaded filenames |

content.text:
I've finished the survey and haven't changed anything. Your rule is already uc-automa's rule and is enforced there. The hyphenated form comes from sat-doc-automa, which states it in several documents and enforces it with a script copied into nine checkouts. 192 files in 8 repositories need renaming, and sat-doc-automa and uc-radar have uncommitted work that overlaps with this change.

## 1. Where the rule is stated

| Where | Says | Agrees? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| uc-automa: directive `naming/versions-in-filenames` 0.1.0, decision 0002, decision 0026, `en-ca/conf/layouts/base.yaml`, the directive templates | dotted below 1.0.0, nothing from 1.0.0, hyphenated "never" | ✅ |
| sat-doc-automa `ROADMAP.md` decision D2 | "Hyphens, always: `v0-1-0`, never `v0.1.0`" | ❌ |
| sat-doc-automa + uc-radar `versioning-postfix-rules-v0-1-0.md` | hyphenated below 1.0.0; drop at 1.0.0 | ❌ separator / ✅ drop at 1.0.0 |
| sat-doc-automa `style-guide--versioned-documents-in-unrendered-markdown-v0-5-0.md` (uc-radar has an older 0.3.0 copy) | "The hyphen separator pattern (`v0-1-0`) is mandatory" | ❌ / ✅ drop at 1.0.0 |
| sat-doc-automa + uc-radar `style-guide--plain-language-…-v0-5-0.md` | `vMAJOR-MINOR-PATCH` | ❌ |
| sat-doc-automa + uc-radar `style-guide--web-ready-…-apa-7-v0-5-0.md` | example `infrastructure-shim-pattern-v0-2-0.md` | ❌ |
| sat-doc-automa `standard-repository-layout-v0-4-0.md` | example `some-document-v0-1-0.md` | ❌ |
| uc-radar `…/eu-ai-act-compliance-file-structure-and-roadmap.md` | restates the hyphenated rule | ❌ |
| uc-radar `en/docs/radar/README.md` | radar entries carry no version suffix at all | ❌ (a different exception) |
| sat-doc-automa, untracked: `markdown--versioned-document-filenames-v0.1.0.md` | `<slug>-v0.1.0.md` | ✅ |
| sat-doc-automa, untracked: same document, `-v0.2.0.md` | adds `<slug>--<variant>--v0.1.0.md` | ⚠️ the double hyphen before `v` differs from your form; it doesn't cover 1.0.0 |

The other repositories state no rule. The overview in uc-automa (`overview--sat-development-current-state`) describes this split already; it's a record "added as issued", so I'd leave it alone.

## 2. Filenames that break the rule

**192 hyphenated files** (all of them below 1.0.0; no dotted postfix at 1.0.0 or later exists anywhere):

| Repository | Files | Of which are shared copies from sat-doc-automa |
| --- | --- | --- |
| uc-radar | 85 (3 are PDFs) | ~10 |
| sat-doc-automa | 30 | it is the source |
| balise-sos-demo | 22 | 7 |
| osat-fluent-restic-tool | 18 | 9 |
| osat-manager-python | 11 | 9 |
| osat-manager-slugify | 10 | 10 |
| uc-cboard | 9 | 9 |
| file-fairy | 7 | 1 |

Eight repositories are clean: uc-automa, uc-portage, uc-processes, uc-test-platform, osat-manager-restic, osat-manager-git, eleventy-website-vishpala-com and followthestack.

Some of these need your call:
- **`-draft` in the name:** uc-radar `universal-cake-evaluation-metrics-v0-4-0-draft.md` and `-v0-5-0-draft.md`.
- **Filename disagrees with front matter:**
  - osat-fluent-restic-tool `restic-backup-guide--…-v0-6-1.md` says 0.6.0 inside.
  - sat-doc-automa `…mermaid…-v0-1-3.md` says 0.1.2 inside.
  - sat-doc-automa `guides/style-guides/…mermaid…-v0-1-5.md` says 0.1.1 inside.
- **8 documents below 1.0.0 with no postfix:** 5 in uc-radar `radar/`, 2 in osat-manager-git and 1 in osat-fluent-restic-tool. The uc-radar ones fall under that README's "no suffix" exception.

## 3. What refers to them

The scan found 687 references to hyphenated names:

| Kind | Count | Proposal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| file-fairy manifests (`source:`/`dest:`): 15 in sat-doc-automa, 1 in file-fairy | 303 | update |
| `.file-fairy-state.yaml`: 5 repositories | 92 | update the keys and `source:` lines |
| Markdown links: balise README 17, sat-doc-automa README 16, osat-fluent-restic-tool 3, osat-manager-python 1, uc-processes 2 (GitHub `blob/main` URLs into uc-radar), uc-radar | 38 | update |
| Front matter: uc-radar `dc:source` ×2 and `relation` ×1; one uc-radar `dcterms:identifier` that includes a version; uc-portage `dc:source` ×2 | 6 | update uc-radar; **leave uc-portage**, since its two point at a fixed commit |
| Paths in prose and `.gitignore` comments | 49 | update |
| History: CHANGELOGs, `git status` listings, `sat:changelog`, Changelog tables | 129 | **leave unchanged** |
| Names of files that don't exist: old versions, examples, broken links | 59 outside history | rule examples get converted; broken links are listed for you |
| uc-automa: counter-examples in the rule, tests, and the overview | 8 | leave unchanged |

## 4. Tooling

- **uc-automa** `conformance.naming.versions_in_filenames` already enforces your rule, including the 1.0.0 half. Nothing to change.
- **`check-conformance.py`** in sat-doc-automa reports a dotted postfix as an error, so it fails the correct form. Its name-to-identifier matching (`slug_from_filename`) accepts both forms. File-fairy copies it into 8 repositories, and the copies are identical (a ninth sits in the non-git `osat-fluent-restic-tool-0.4.4`).
- **file-fairy** and its manifests generate the destination filenames. Most manifests point at `~/2-areas/development/...` targets that don't exist on this machine, so running `ff apply` won't carry the renames.
- `bump-version.py`, `cut-release.py`, `normalize-metadata.py` and `publish-release.py` never touch document filenames.

## 5. Proposed changes

One branch per repository, `dotted-version-postfixes`, from `origin/main`, each in its own worktree beside the repository. That keeps your checkouts and uncommitted work untouched.

1. **Rule documents in sat-doc-automa:**
   - Restate `versioning-postfix-rules` with dots, as 0.2.0. Keeping the drop-at-1.0.0 half means it covers more than your draft does.
   - Rewrite the file-naming sections of the versioned-documents, plain-language and APA-7 style guides and the layout standard, each with a minor version bump and a Changelog row.
   - Add a new ROADMAP entry that supersedes D2, and mark D2 as superseded rather than rewriting it.
   - The same edits go into the uc-radar copies, plus the eu-ai-act roadmap paragraph.
2. **`check-conformance.py`:** report `-vX-Y-Z` and accept dots. The same file then goes to all 8 copies.
3. **Renames:** 192 `git mv` commands, all listed in the rename plan file (path at the end). PDFs move with their Markdown files.
4. **References:** update everything in the "update" rows of section 3, in the same commit as the renames, per repository.

    A document whose only change is a corrected link keeps its version. A version bump would rename it again.

## Decisions I need from you

1. **Your uncommitted work.** In sat-doc-automa, 7 hyphenated defaults are deleted, with dotted copies untracked. In uc-radar, files are moved into `artifacts/` and new 0.2.0, 0.3.0 and 0.6.0 versions exist. osat-manager-python is on `windows-test-fixes` with dotted and hyphenated files untracked. Should you commit those first so I build on them, or should I branch from `origin/main` and you reconcile afterwards?
2. **Two directives in sat-doc-automa.** Keep `versioning-postfix-rules` and retire or merge your `markdown--versioned-document-filenames` draft, or the reverse? Is the 0.2.0 `--variant--v0.1.0` form wanted? It isn't `<title-slug>-v0.1.0.md`.
3. **`-draft` files:** rename them to `-v0.4.0.md` and `-v0.5.0.md`? The status would then live only in front matter.
4. **Mismatched versions (3 files):** rename keeping the filename's version and leave the contents for you, or fix one side?
5. **Documents with no postfix (8):** rename them in this change, or keep uc-radar's radar-entry exception and handle these separately?
6. **Shared copies:** rename them directly in each repository and update its state file (my recommendation), or change only sat-doc-automa and its manifests?
7. **Broken references** to files that don't exist: leave them as they are, or point them at the current versions where that's obvious (for example uc-radar `en/docs/README.md` links to style guides at 0.2.0 when 0.5.0 exists)?

The working lists are in my scratchpad:
- Rename plan: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-initial-areas-development-uc-automa/9d1a7251-5a7a-4a89-96d6-ee6f0ab0a8bf/scratchpad/rename-plan.tsv`
- Every reference, classified: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-initial-areas-development-uc-automa/9d1a7251-5a7a-4a89-96d6-ee6f0ab0a8bf/scratchpad/refs-classified.tsv`
- Filename versus front matter: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-initial-areas-development-uc-automa/9d1a7251-5a7a-4a89-96d6-ee6f0ab0a8bf/scratchpad/survey.tsv`

#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""
cut-release.py, cut a release: bump VERSION, roll CHANGELOG.md's
Unreleased section into a dated version section, commit surgically, tag,
and stop before push.
This script owns the release ceremony only. Version arithmetic stays in
bump-version.py, which this script calls rather than reimplements, so
there is exactly one place that computes "what's the next version."
Document versions under en/docs/ are independent of the repository
version, per CONTRIBUTORS.md, and are never touched here. The only
content this script writes is mechanical: renaming CHANGELOG.md's
`## [Unreleased]` heading into a dated `## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD` heading
and leaving a fresh empty Unreleased section above it, per Keep a
Changelog. The entries themselves, what actually changed, are written by
hand as work happens; this script never composes changelog prose.
Usage:
    cut-release.py patch      0.1.0 -> 0.1.1
    cut-release.py minor      0.1.1 -> 0.2.0
    cut-release.py major      0.2.0 -> 1.0.0
    cut-release.py 0.3.2      set an explicit version
Sequence: guard (VERSION clean, Unreleased section has content) -> bump
(via bump-version.py) -> roll Unreleased into a dated version section in
CHANGELOG.md -> surgical commit (VERSION and CHANGELOG.md only, never
`git add .`) -> guard (HEAD:VERSION) -> annotated tag -> guard
(tag:VERSION) -> report. It stops before push; pushing stays a
deliberate act:
    git push && git push origin vX.Y.Z
Refusals: a dirty VERSION before starting (a half-done release is
finished, not built upon); an empty or missing Unreleased section

## Rule

- A release tag is `v` followed by the contents of `VERSION`, with dots, as in filename suffixes: `v0.1.0`, never `0.1.0` or `v0-1-0`. Every tag in a repository is a release tag.
- Release tags are annotated, and the message names the repository and the version, such as `uc-automa 0.1.0`.
- The tag points at the release commit, whose `VERSION` is that version and whose `CHANGELOG.md` has the section `## [0.1.0] - 2026-10-09`, dated the day the tag was made, in local time.
- The release commit is surgical: it changes only `CHANGELOG.md`, `VERSION` if it needed changing, and in `README.md` the references that install the repository's own release (the directive `release/readme-install-tag`), so the tag marks exactly the release.
- Keep a Changelog's link references at the end of the changelog are left out until the repository has a remote for them to point at.

Signed tags come with the release ceremony, planned for uc-automa 0.2.0.

## Rationale

Christopher Steel set this rule on 2026-10-09, when uc-portage and uc-automa were first tagged. A tag that matches its `VERSION` and changelog lets anyone go from a release to exactly what it contained.

## Examples

| Tag | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| annotated `v0.1.0`, message `uc-portage 0.1.0`, at a commit with `VERSION` 0.1.0 and `## [0.1.0] - 2026-10-09` | Conforms |
| lightweight `v0.1.0` | Not annotated |
| `0.1.0` or `v0-1-0` | Wrong form |
| `v0.1.0` at a commit whose `VERSION` is 0.2.0 | Does not match |

## Check

`conformance.release.annotated_version_tags` checks every tag of a git repository; outside git it has nothing to check. Its fixtures are under `tests/fixtures/conformance/release/annotated-version-tags/`, each a small repository kept as a git bundle and cloned by the tests.

## Changelog

| Version | Date | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.1.0 | 2026-10-09 | In force | Initial version |
| 0.2.0 | 2026-10-11 | In force | The release commit may also update `README.md`'s install references to the new tag |

"""

lines = sec.split("\n")

# step back over blank line before ### Changed
j = i - 1
while lines[j] == "": j -= 1
lines[j+1:j+1] = added.rstrip("\n").split("\n")

# find end of Changed list
k = i + 1

-# Overview: SAT Development, Current State
-Version: 0.1.0
-Status: Draft
-## Purpose and scope

-SAT development already runs on a coherent system: sat-doc-automa holds the canonical conventions and scripts, file-fairy distributes them, and product repositories receive them. The system is unevenly applied, and its procedures for new repositories, test platforms and releases are not yet written down in one place.

-This document records how things work today, as observed in the public repositories on 2026-10-07. It describes rather than prescribes. Findings are collected near the end as input for a separate improvement pass.

-In scope: sat-doc-automa, uc-radar, file-fairy, osat-manager-python and the other OSAT Fluent tools, sat, satx, and balise-sos-demo. Out of scope for now: client hosting, and websites not yet in a public repository.
-## The system at a glance
-Conventions and scripts move one way, from sat-doc-automa through file-fairy into each repository. Nothing carries product decisions back to the radar.
-```mermaid
-flowchart LR

- radar["uc-radar
Evaluates tools and approaches
Rings: adopt, assess, hold"]

- automa["sat-doc-automa
House rules and guides
Release ceremony scripts
One manifest per target"]

- osat["OSAT managers
User-space runtimes
manage-python 1.0"]

- fairy["file-fairy
plan, apply, status
Checksum drift record"]
-    subgraph targets["Receiving repositories"]
-        t1["uc-radar"]
-        t2["osat-manager-python"]
-        t3["file-fairy"]
-        t4["sat"]
-        t5["balise-sos-demo"]
-        t6["satx"]
-    end
-    radar -- adopts --> automa
-    automa -- manifests --> fairy
-    osat -- runtime --> fairy
-    fairy -- sync --> targets
-    targets -. "stack decisions in product ADRs do not return" .-> radar
-    classDef synced fill:#d8f0d8,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#000
-    classDef partial fill:#fff1cc,stroke:#b58100,color:#000
-    classDef none fill:#f8d7d7,stroke:#b3261e,color:#000
-    class t1,t2 synced
-    class t3,t4 partial
-    class t5,t6 none
-Key: green means synced with a state file recorded; amber means a manifest exists but no sync record was seen; red means no manifest in the automa.

-The radar decides what is adopted, the automa holds the canonical files, file-fairy distributes them on the runtimes the OSAT managers install, and the products receive them. Coverage is uneven: two targets show a sync record, two have a manifest but no record, and two have no manifest at all.
-## Resources
-Seven repositories carry the work, in three roles: governance (automa, radar), tooling (file-fairy, OSAT managers) and products (SAT, Balise).
-### sat-doc-automa, the canonical source
-sat-doc-automa [(Steel, 2026e)](#ref-steel-2026e) is the canonical home for style guides, formats, templates and automa across SAT, OSAT Fluent and Universal Cake. It holds:

-- Automa under `en/docs/automa/`, per format, with `defaults/` for rules in force and `examples/` for chosen alternatives: markdown rules, AI collaboration, licence blocks, and the shared CLAUDE.md signpost block.

-- Guides: five style guides (versioned documents, technical register, plain language, navigation and accessibility, APA 7) and the devops guides (Commit and Versioning Workflow v0-3-0, file-fairy Usage v0-1-0).
-- Decision records under `en/docs/decisions/devops/`, including gh CLI for release asset publishing.
-- The release ceremony scripts at the root: `bump-version.py`, `cut-release.py`, `publish-release.py`, `check-conformance.py`, `test_publish_release.py`, plus `normalize-metadata.py`.
-- Eleven file-fairy manifests, `ff-manifest-<target>.yaml`, one per receiving repository.
-It is deliberately structured as a SAT archive from its first commit, so it can become the first SAT archive with little rework.
-### uc-radar, the decision gate

-uc-radar [(Steel, 2026g)](#ref-steel-2026g) holds Universal Cake radar entries and the evaluation metrics. Entries sit under `en/docs/radar/` in rings `adopt/`, `assess/` and `hold/`, grouped by domain. Process documents live beside them: an evaluation lifecycle (v0-1-0), an entry template (v0-2-0) and a praxis evaluation prompt (v0-1-1). Metrics versions v0-3-1, v0-4-0-draft, v0-5-0-draft and v0-5-1 are all present. The current release is 0.2.4 (2026-09-29). It has received the shared zone from sat-doc-automa through file-fairy since 0.1.2 [(Steel, 2026h)](#ref-steel-2026h).
-### file-fairy, the distribution mechanism

-file-fairy [(Steel, 2026b)](#ref-steel-2026b) is a manifest-driven CLI with `plan`, `apply` and `status` verbs. It copies named groups of files from a source repository to a target on local disk and tracks drift by checksum in a per-target `.file-fairy-state.yaml`. Sync modes are `mirror` (the default), `seed_if_missing`, `overwrite` and `reference_only`. It also supports retraction (`state: absent`) and managed blocks inside files the target otherwise owns. It started as a radar entry, and it needs Python 3.8+ and PyYAML.
-### OSAT managers, the runtimes

-osat-manager-python [(Steel, 2026c)](#ref-steel-2026c), run as `manage-python`, installs self-contained CPython runtimes into user space without elevated privilege, a package manager or a compiler. It is at 1.0.x, verified end to end on Linux x86-64; the Windows aliases, `install.ps1` and macOS are not yet verified. It is the first of the OSAT collection to move from `-tool` installer to `-manager`. Siblings with manifests in the automa include the hugo, myrepos, rclone, restic, sat and wekan tools.
-### sat, the current SAT line

-sat [(Steel, 2026d)](#ref-steel-2026d) is Source Archive Tools: filesystem-first archive management with small standalone commands. Its README status reads `sat_version: 0.7.0`. It carries the content pipeline (metadata ingress, egress, transmog to MkDocs), `satlib`, and docs under `en/`. Tools live under `en/bin` and `en/lib`. -## The shared repository kit
-A de facto standard repository already exists: the same root files recur across most repositories, delivered by file-fairy from sat-doc-automa.
-| File or path | Role | Delivered how |
-| `VERSION` | Single source of the version | Seeded once, then owned by the repo (`seed_if_missing` is the documented example) |
-| `CHANGELOG.md` | Repository changelog, Keep a Changelog format | Per repo |
-| `ROADMAP.md` | Forward plan | Per repo |
-| `CLAUDE.md` | AI collaboration signpost | Shared signpost block from `automa/claude-md/` |
-| `LICENSE` | Licence text | Per repo; licence blocks from `automa/licenses/` |
-| `bump-version.py` | Computes and writes the next version | Synced from automa, devops-scripts group |
-| `cut-release.py` | Bump, roll changelog, surgical commit, tag, stop before push | Synced from automa |
-| `publish-release.py` | Tarball, `SHA256SUMS`, optional GPG, via `gh` or a plain directory | Synced from automa |
-| `check-conformance.py` | Lints markdown against house rules | Synced from automa |
-| `test_publish_release.py` | Offline tests for the publish ceremony | Synced from automa |
-| `normalize-metadata.py` | Metadata normalisation | Present in automa, uc-radar, osat-manager-python; not listed in the automa README |
-| `.file-fairy-state.yaml` | Record of the last sync | Written by file-fairy in the target |
-| `en/docs/` | Language-rooted documentation | Convention, plus synced devops guides and automa |

-Per-document conventions ride on top: Dublin Core and `sat:` front matter, versioned filenames (the spec is `-vX.Y.Z` before 1.0.0 and no version in the filename from 1.0.0; most repositories currently use `-vX-Y-Z`), a changelog table in each document, and a License section built from the licence blocks.
-## Procedures as practised

-Only the release ceremony and the sync are written down. New repository and test platform setup are reconstructed here from what the repositories contain, and steps marked (inferred) need confirming.
-### New repository
-1. Create the repository on GitHub under steelcj and clone it locally (inferred).
-2. Write a manifest `ff-manifest-<repo>.yaml` in sat-doc-automa naming the groups the repo receives.
-3. Run `file-fairy plan`, then `file-fairy apply`, against the manifest.
-4. Commit what arrived as its own commit, the receive-then-commit pattern in the file-fairy Usage guide; uc-radar records this as a changelog entry.
-5. Add the repo's own `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `ROADMAP.md` and `en/docs/` content (inferred).
-### Keeping a repository current
-1. Change the canonical file in sat-doc-automa.
-2. Run `file-fairy plan` per manifest to see `new`, `update` and `conflict` items.
-3. Run `apply`; conflicts on `mirror` items are skipped unless `--force` is given.
-4. Commit the received files in each target.
-There is no single command that runs every manifest, so propagation depends on remembering which targets exist (inferred).
-### Release
-From the Commit and Versioning Workflow v0-3-0, the ceremony in four steps:
-1. Write the changelog entries under `[Unreleased]`.
-2. Run `cut-release.py`: bump, roll the changelog, surgical commit, tag, stop before push.
-3. Push the commit and the tag.
-4. Run `publish-release.py`: deterministic tarball, `SHA256SUMS`, optional GPG signature, published with `gh` or to a plain directory.
-sat predates the synced kit and uses its own `bump-sat-version.py`.
-### Test platforms
-Three kinds are in use, each set up per project:
-- Unit and offline tests in the repo root, run with `python3 test_*.py` (file-fairy, osat-manager-python, and the publish ceremony everywhere).
-- End-to-end runs on Linux, such as `e2e_manage_python.py`, presumably inside Incus containers on flow (inferred).
-- Windows 11 VM validation through `validate-windows.ps1` in osat-manager-python.
-Balise adds `npm run check`: an offline link check and markdown conformance.
-### Publishing a site

-Balise builds with `npm run build` into `_site/` and deploys with `npm run deploy:local` to an Incus web container on flow.local. ADR-006 records the choice of self-hosted publishing without GitHub Actions. sat's README shows the older path: `archive-init.py` creating a MkDocs docs tree for chrissteel.com.

-# Moving Universal Cake Tools to GPL-2.0
-10 Oct 2026 · @sirhc
-## Summary

-Moving the Universal Cake tools from AGPL-3.0-or-later to GPL-2.0 would make them easier for cautious organizations to adopt, but it would remove the protection that matters most for a hosted radar: the right of network users to get the source. GPL-2.0 also lacks an explicit patent grant, is not compatible with Apache-2.0 code, and breaks the CC BY-SA 4.0 bridge that runs only to GPLv3.

-The draft conclusion is to keep AGPL-3.0-or-later for anything run as a service, and to consider GPL-3.0-or-later, not GPL-2.0, for tools that are only ever distributed and run locally. This stays provisional until the licensing owner confirms it.
-## What would change
-The biggest difference is the network clause; most of the others follow from GPLv3 being written 16 years after GPLv2.
-| Term                                                         | AGPL-3.0-or-later (current)   | GPL-2.0-only           | GPL-2.0-or-later        |
-| Source owed to network users of a modified version           | Yes, section 13               | No                     | No                      |
-| Source owed when copies are distributed                      | Yes                           | Yes                    | Yes                     |
-| Explicit patent licence from contributors                    | Yes                           | No, implied at best    | No, implied at best     |
-| Anti-tivoization (installation information for consumer devices) | Yes                           | No                     | No                      |
-| Cure period after a violation                                | Yes, 30 and 60 day provisions | No, rights end at once | No, rights end at once  |
-| Can move to a future licence version                         | Yes                           | No                     | Yes, to GPLv3 and later |
-| Combinable with GPLv3 or AGPLv3 code                         | Yes                           | No                     | Yes, by choosing v3     |
-| Combinable with Apache-2.0 code                              | Yes                           | No, in the FSF's view  | Yes, by choosing v3     |
-## Advantages of GPL-2.0
-The case for GPL-2.0 is mostly about adoption and simplicity, not stronger protection.
-- Fewer policy blocks. Many companies and some public bodies ban AGPL code outright but allow GPL-2.0, so procurement and IT reviews get shorter.
-- Lighter duties for clients who host. A municipality or NGO that modifies a tool and runs it internally or on a public site would owe source only if it distributed copies, not to every visitor.
-- Familiarity. GPL-2.0 is the licence of the Linux kernel and has decades of case history and community practice behind it.
-- Shorter text. GPL-2.0 is about half the length of AGPLv3 and easier to explain to a non-specialist client.
-- Fixed terms (GPL-2.0-only). No future licence version can change what contributors agreed to, which is the reason Linus Torvalds keeps the kernel on version 2 only.
-- Kernel and embedded alignment. Code that might one day be shared with GPL-2.0-only projects, such as kernel modules or some embedded firmware, can be combined directly.
-## Disadvantages of GPL-2.0
-The main cost is that a hosted fork could stay closed, which is the exact risk the AGPL was chosen to prevent.
-- The network gap. A vendor or consultancy could modify `uc-radar`, run it as a paid rating service and never publish its changes. GPL-2.0 is triggered by distributing copies, not by serving users.
-- No explicit patent grant. Contributors do not expressly licence their patents, and there is no patent retaliation clause, so downstream users of a tool have weaker protection.
-- Harsh termination. Any violation ends a licensee's rights immediately, with no cure period, which is a poor fit for small organizations that make honest mistakes.
-- No anti-tivoization. A device maker could ship a modified tool on locked hardware that users cannot update, which works against agency and longevity.
-- Compatibility losses. GPL-2.0-only cannot be combined with GPLv3, AGPLv3 or Apache-2.0 code, which rules out a large share of modern libraries (Apache Software Foundation, n.d.).
-- Dated wording. GPLv2 was written around US concepts like "distribution"; GPLv3 uses "convey" and "propagate" to work more evenly across jurisdictions, including Canada.
-- Mixed signals. A practice that scores vendors on sovereignty would be choosing a weaker copyleft for its own hosted tools.
-## Compatibility
-GPL-2.0-only is the most isolated option here: it combines with GPL-2.0 and permissive code, but not with any version 3 licence, Apache-2.0 or CC BY-SA content.
-| Other licence        | With AGPL-3.0-or-later | With GPL-2.0-only | With GPL-2.0-or-later  |
-| MIT, BSD             | Yes                    | Yes               | Yes                    |
-| Apache-2.0           | Yes                    | No, per the FSF   | Yes, if released as v3 |
-| GPL-2.0-only         | No                     | Yes               | Yes, as v2             |
-| GPL-3.0              | Yes, via section 13    | No                | Yes, as v3             |
-| CC BY-SA 4.0 content | Yes, via GPLv3         | No                | Yes, as v3             |

-The FSF has never accepted Apache-2.0 as compatible with GPLv2, because of Apache's patent termination and indemnification terms, while Apache-2.0 code can go into GPLv3 works (Apache Software Foundation, n.d.). CC BY-SA 4.0 is one-way compatible with GPLv3 only (Creative Commons, 2015), so the content-to-code bridge in the licensing rationale would not survive a GPL-2.0-only move.
-## Against the Universal Cake metrics

-Scored against its own criteria, GPL-2.0 does slightly better on ease of adoption and worse on agency, sovereignty, privacy and longevity. The ratings below are a qualitative draft, not a formal radar evaluation.
-| Criterion                          | AGPL-3.0-or-later | GPL-2.0  | Why                                                          |
-| Agency                             | Stronger          | Weaker   | Users of a hosted fork keep the right to its source only under AGPL |
-| Sovereignty                        | Stronger          | Weaker   | Clients can always take a hosted tool in house only if its source is owed |
-| Privacy                            | Stronger          | Weaker   | Users can audit what a hosted fork does with their data only if they get the source |
-| Security                           | Stronger          | Weaker   | Explicit patent terms and source for hosted forks support independent review |
-| Longevity                          | Stronger          | Mixed    | Or-later allows upgrades; GPL-2.0-only freezes terms but also blocks v3 libraries |
-| Inclusive design                   | Neutral           | Neutral  | Licence choice does not change accessibility directly        |
-| Multilingual support               | Neutral           | Neutral  | Both allow translation of interfaces and docs                |
-| Environment                        | Neutral           | Neutral  | No direct effect                                             |
-| Adoption by cautious organizations | Weaker            | Stronger | AGPL bans are common in corporate policy                     |
-## Relicensing in practice
-A change is only possible for code whose copyright holders all agree, and it never takes back copies already released under AGPL.
-- Sole authorship. Code written only by the practice can be relicensed by the practice at any time.
-- Outside contributions. Every external contributor must agree, unless they signed a contributor agreement allowing it. Without that, their code stays AGPL and must be rewritten or removed.
-- AGPL dependencies. Any AGPL or GPLv3 library a tool depends on must be replaced, because GPL-2.0-only cannot include it.
-- Existing releases stay AGPL. Anyone holding an AGPL copy can keep using and forking it under AGPL; only new versions change.
-- Repository hygiene. Each repository needs updated `LICENSE` files, SPDX identifiers in file headers, licence statements in the documentation front matter, and a changelog entry.
-## Options and open questions

-If the goal is easier adoption, GPL-3.0-or-later for locally run tools gets most of that benefit without giving up patent terms or compatibility; GPL-2.0 is hard to justify unless a tool must combine with GPL-2.0-only code.
-| Option                 | Network protection | Adoption | Compatibility | Fits when                                                    |
-| Keep AGPL-3.0-or-later | Yes                | Lowest   | Broad         | Tools run as hosted services, such as the radar site         |
-| GPL-3.0-or-later       | No                 | Higher   | Broad         | Command-line and build tools only run locally                |
-| GPL-2.0-or-later       | No                 | Higher   | Broad, via v3 | Code that may be shared with both v2-only and v3 projects    |
-| GPL-2.0-only           | No                 | Higher   | Narrow        | Code that must link with the Linux kernel or other v2-only projects |
-| Dual AGPL plus GPL-2.0 | Reuser's choice    | Highest  | Broad         | Rarely worth it; reusers pick the weaker licence             |
-Open questions:
-- Which tools run as hosted services, and which are only distributed?
-- Has any outside contributor's code been merged that would need consent?
-- Does any tool need to combine with GPL-2.0-only code today?
-- Have specific clients or partners raised AGPL as a blocker?
-This is a rationale, not legal advice; a lawyer familiar with Canadian copyright should review any change.
-## References
-Apache Software Foundation. (n.d.). *Apache License v2.0 and GPL compatibility*. Retrieved October 10, 2026, from https://www.apache.org/licenses/GPL-compatibility.html
-Creative Commons. (2015, October 8). *CC BY-SA 4.0 now one-way compatible with GPLv3*. https://creativecommons.org/2015/10/08/cc-by-sa-4-0-now-one-way-compatible-with-gplv3/
-Free Software Foundation. (1991). *GNU General Public License, version 2*. https://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/gpl-2.0.html
